title: The Upside-Down Drinker
twist: Most people think food and drink fall down into the stomach. They don't: muscles squeeze them along, which is why Leila — and astronauts in space — can swallow upside down.
briefing: Leila, 14, is at gymnastics camp. Her teammates bet she can't drink water while holding a handstand against the wall. She sips through a straw, swallows, and the water ends up in her stomach — not back in her mouth or nose.
question: How did the water go up into her stomach?

clues.title: Water went 'up'
clues.text: Upside down, her stomach was higher than her mouth. She swallowed three sips comfortably, with no coughing at all.
clues.shows: liquid travelling upward into her stomach

clues.title: Astronauts do it
clues.text: Her coach shows a video of astronauts on a space station eating and swallowing with no gravity pulling anything down.
clues.shows: swallowing working with no gravity at all

clues.title: A ripple in the throat
clues.text: A teammate watches her neck: after each swallow a squeezing ripple moves down it. Leila can feel it pushing, like toothpaste squeezed along a tube.
clues.shows: a wave of muscle squeezing along the food tube

clues.title: A bit slower upside down
clues.text: Upright, a sip takes about six seconds to reach her stomach. Upside down it takes a few seconds longer — around eight or nine — but it still gets there.
clues.shows: gravity helping a little when upright, but not being needed

hypotheses.text: Swallowing is done by muscles: rings of muscle in the food tube squeeze in a wave that pushes food and water to the stomach, so it works whichever way up you are — gravity only helps a little.
She was lucky — some water probably went into her nose or lungs.
hypotheses.flaw: Water going the wrong way makes you cough and splutter at once; she swallowed comfortably and felt it reach her stomach.

hypotheses.text: Gravity pulls water into the stomach, so it must have flowed down somehow.
hypotheses.flaw: Upside down, gravity pulls toward her head, away from her stomach — and astronauts swallow with no gravity at all.

hypotheses.text: The straw pushed the water down for her.
hypotheses.flaw: A straw only gets water into the mouth; the ripple in her throat did the rest, and astronauts swallow without straws.

transfer.context: At the zoo, Orla watches a giraffe drink from a pond. Its head is far below its stomach, yet the water travels all the way up its long neck.
options: Giraffes have a special pump in their mouths.
Muscle waves in the giraffe's long food tube squeeze the water upward to its stomach.
The giraffe holds its breath, which sucks the water up.
Gravity pulls the water toward the giraffe's stomach.
transfer.retryHint: What did Leila's teammate see moving along her neck after every swallow?
transfer.explanation: The giraffe's food tube works just like Leila's: rings of muscle squeeze in a wave, pushing water uphill to the stomach. Gravity is pulling the wrong way, so the muscles do all the work.

takeaway: Swallowing is a muscle job, not a gravity job. Rings of muscle squeeze food and drink along in a wave — which is why astronauts can eat in space and you can swallow upside down.
